name: Kira Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a big iron ore pit, and these days I run blast-hole drills, the rigs that drill the holes for the explosives on each bench. Three years ago they made two of our drills semi-autonomous, so now I sit in one cab and keep an eye on the other two on a tablet. They drill their own pattern, and I step in when one gets stuck on a hard band of rock or the GPS drops out. The heat on the benches in January is brutal, and the drills still need a human more often than the brochure says.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up being the one running three drills?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I put my hand up. I've been on drills twenty-six years, I'm the senior operator on our crew, and when the trial came along most of the old hands didn't want it. I'd already been using AI on my phone for years, writing my shift reports, checking pattern maths, even planning my wife Joan's birthday dinner. So I thought, if it's coming, I'd rather be the one teaching it than the one replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a bit of a letdown, honestly. I'd say it at work with a laugh, because half the crew would be pleased to see me proved wrong. Online I'd probably post something about how the tools are still useful even if they're not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it changes nothing for me. I'd still run my three drills, still use the AI for reports, and still retire in about five years with a good pension and a paid-off house. I might be a bit bored, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, and keep using the AI tools every day. I'd probably push the company to finish the drill automation they started, because the semi-autonomous rigs do save us time on the bench. I'd also keep up the union work on fatigue rules, which matters whatever happens with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a touch of disappointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Disappointment is an unusual answer. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen what these tools can do on a good day, and I'd hoped they'd take the worst parts of the job off us. The heat, the dust, the night shifts. If it all stalls, the young ones are still doing what I did in 1999.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your crew would be pleased to see you proved wrong. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Greg, mostly. He's run a drill for thirty years and calls my tablet the babysitter. He'd buy me a beer and never let me forget it.

S0.say: I'd tell the crew with a laugh that it's a letdown, knowing half of them would enjoy seeing me proved wrong. Online I'd post that the tools are still useful even if they aren't magic.
S0.think: Privately nothing changes for me, I'd still run three drills and retire in about five years with good savings and a paid-off house. I might just be a bit bored.
S0.do: Keeps running her drills and using AI tools daily. Pushes the company to finish the drill automation it started and keeps up union work on fatigue rules.
S0.feel: Calm, with a touch of disappointment.
S0.quote: If it all stalls, the young ones are still doing what I did in 1999.
S0.fieldNote: Kira is the rare worker who would be disappointed if AI stalled, because she hoped it would remove the worst parts of the job. She already supervises semi-autonomous drills and treats it as normal. Her progressive streak shows in her focus on the young workers and fatigue rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, as long as the workers share in it. If one person can run three drills, the company's saving a fortune, and some of that should come back as shorter rosters or better pay. I'd say that at the union meeting and I'd post it online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm well placed. I'm already doing the job they'd want everyone doing. My worry is for the others on the crew who've refused to touch the tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to train the rest of the crew on the semi-autonomous rigs, and I'd ask for a trainer's allowance for it. I'd push our union to bargain for what I call an automation dividend, so if a crew's output goes up from automation, the roster goes down, like from four on to three on. And I'd keep learning whatever new system comes in first, because that's where I'm most useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. Steady Disruption is pretty much what I'd hoped for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Greg, who calls your tablet the babysitter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with him for a shift and show him it does the boring holes so he can deal with the tricky ones. He's the best I've seen at reading broken ground. If he refuses, I'd help him get a spot on the manual rigs until he retires, because he's earned that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask for a trainer's allowance. Is money a driver for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, we're comfortable. But if I don't ask, the next woman they ask to train people won't get it either. It's about setting the rate, not about me.

S1.say: I'd say it's good as long as workers share in it, through shorter rosters or better pay when one person can run three drills. I'd say it at the union meeting and post it online.
S1.think: Privately I'm well placed, because I'm already doing the job they'd want everyone doing. My worry is for crew members who refuse to touch the tablet.
S1.do: Volunteers to train the crew on semi-autonomous rigs and asks for a trainer's allowance. Pushes the union to bargain for an automation dividend, such as cutting the roster from four days on to three.
S1.feel: Calm and even a bit excited, since this is close to what she hoped for.
S1.quote: If I don't ask, the next woman they ask to train people won't get it either.
S1.fieldNote: Kira combines early adoption with a strong belief that the gains should be shared, which is a less common mix. Her idea of an automation dividend is concrete and well thought out. She shows real loyalty to Greg, the colleague who mocks her, and wants to protect him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one's too fast, even for me. I'd say governments need to move now on income support and retraining, because companies won't do it on their own in two years. I'd post about it, I'd write to my member of parliament, and I'd push the union to go public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I'd be fine. I'd be sixty, with savings, and honestly I'd probably be one of the last people they'd let go, because someone has to watch the machines in the first year. But I'd be watching most of my crew lose their jobs while I kept mine, and that would sit badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the company in the first month and offer to help commission the fully autonomous drills, on a contract if they wanted, so the rollout is done safely and with people who know the ground. I'd also use some of our savings to help set up a crew fund with the union, to help people with mortgages through the gap. And I'd be at every meeting pushing the government for a transition payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared for me, but it's a heavy thing to be the one who's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having only two years change things, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, the crew can't retrain in time, and the technical college can't even write the courses that fast. In the slower ones I could help bring people along. In this one, the best I can do is soften the landing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd help commission the machines that replace your crew. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about that a lot. If I don't do it, someone from the vendor flies in who's never been on our benches, and it's done worse and less safely. I'd rather it be me, and I'd be upfront with the crew about why.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast even for me, and governments must act now on income support and retraining. I'd post about it, write to my member of parliament and push the union to go public.
S2.think: Privately I'd be fine at sixty with savings, and probably among the last let go because someone has to watch the machines. But watching most of my crew lose their jobs while I kept mine would sit badly.
S2.do: Offers within the first month to help commission fully autonomous drills, possibly on contract, so the rollout is safe. Puts some savings into a union crew fund for workers with mortgages and campaigns for a government transition payment.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not afraid for herself but weighed down by being the one who's fine.
S2.quote: I'm not scared for me, but it's a heavy thing to be the one who's fine.
S2.fieldNote: This picture gave Kira a moral problem rather than a money problem: she would help commission the machines that replace her crew. She faced the contradiction directly and had a clear reason. Her willingness to put her own savings into a crew fund stood out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if we start now. Retraining, a transition payment, and the union at the table for every rollout. I'd say it everywhere, at work, online, to the local paper if they asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's actually a good fit. I'd be sixty-three by 2031, which is around when I'd planned to retire anyway. I could spend those years helping set up the autonomous fleet and training people for the jobs around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a short course on autonomous mining systems at the technical college, the online version, so I've got a ticket to go with the experience. Then I'd ask for a formal role as the crew's automation trainer. After I retire, I'd probably do some contract training for other sites, a couple of weeks at a time, which would keep my brain busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit of purpose, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra three years change compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between softening the landing and actually building a runway. With five years, Greg can retire on his own terms, and the younger ones can move into the control room or maintenance on the robots. Nobody has to be thrown out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Joan support you doing contract work after you retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd laugh and say she knew I'd never really retire. She's a science teacher, she gets it. As long as I'm home for her school holidays, she's happy.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough if we start now, with retraining, a transition payment and the union at the table for every rollout. I'd say it at work, online and to the local paper.
S3.think: Privately it's a good fit, since I'd be sixty-three by 2031, about when I planned to retire. I could spend those years setting up the autonomous fleet and training people.
S3.do: Takes an online course in autonomous mining systems at the technical college in the first year and asks for a formal automation trainer role. Plans contract training work for other sites after retiring.
S3.feel: Calm, with a sense of purpose.
S3.quote: It's the difference between softening the landing and actually building a runway.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Kira from uneasy to purposeful, because she can bring her crew along rather than watch them go. She would formalise her skills with a course even at this late stage. Her plan for contract training after retirement shows she sees herself working well past her official end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse to leave anyone behind. I'd push for it to be planned like a public project, with the union, the companies and the government all at the table. And I'd say it loudly, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd have retired by then, or be doing a bit of training work. It doesn't threaten me at all. What I'd think about is whether the gains go to everyone or just to the shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire around 2031 as planned, and in the years before, I'd help write the training material for the autonomous drills at our site. I'd get involved with the union's policy group on automation, which I've been meaning to join. And I'd encourage my son Rafael, who's a mechanic in the city, to learn robot maintenance, because that's going to be busy work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels manageable, maybe even good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to who gets the gains. Why does that matter to you so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I watched the price of iron ore triple once, and the bonuses went to head office while we got a barbecue. If machines are doing the work, the question is who owns the machines. That's the whole thing, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rafael, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the robots will break down, they always do, and someone has to fix them at two in the morning. Learn that, and you'll never be short of work. I'd send him the course link that night.

S4.say: I'd say a decade leaves no excuse to leave anyone behind, and it should be planned like a public project with the union, companies and government. I'd say it loudly, as usual.
S4.think: Privately I'd be retired or doing some training work, so it doesn't threaten me. What I'd think about is whether the gains go to everyone or only to shareholders.
S4.do: Retires around 2031, first helping write training material for the autonomous drills at her site. Joins the union's automation policy group and urges her son Rafael to learn robot maintenance.
S4.feel: Calm, feeling it is manageable and maybe even good.
S4.quote: I watched the price of iron ore triple once, and the bonuses went to head office while we got a barbecue.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Kira's attention turns fully to fairness and ownership. The story about the iron ore boom explained her politics better than any slogan. She gave practical career advice to her son with no sign of fear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's the only one where I can't help the crew move with it. What would help is a transition payment from the government, for a year or two, so people with mortgages aren't panicking while they retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the machines. Everyone asks if robots will take the jobs, and nobody asks who'll be paid for the robots' work. If machines are doing the work, the question is who owns the machines.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if robots will take the jobs, and nobody asks who'll be paid for the robots' work.
portrait: Kira Silva is a 58-year-old senior blast-hole drill operator at an iron ore pit who already supervises two semi-autonomous drills from a tablet and uses AI every day. She is secure, with good savings and a paid-off house, and stays calm through most pictures, even disappointed in AI Plateau that the hard parts of the job would remain. Her worry is fairness: in AGI by 2028 she would be the one who keeps her job while her crew loses theirs, and she would help commission the machines rather than leave it to outsiders. She wants workers to share in the gains through shorter rosters, a crew fund and government transition payments.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it is the only picture where she couldn't help her crew move with the change.
whatWouldHelp: A government transition payment for a year or two so people with mortgages can retrain without panicking.
